A 112 × 112 canvas with a guide at pivot:
File > New, 112 × 112, RGB, transparent background. Save it as a template and reuse it — a sprite drawn on the wrong canvas is wrong at every later stage.

The pivot is (56, 96): horizontal centre, 16 px up from the bottom. That is where the feet stand and where Godot puts the collision origin. Mark it on a guide layer you hide before export, or a single magenta pixel on a layer named "pivot" that you delete when done.

Why 96 and not 112: the frame keeps room below the feet for shadows and for poses that drop. §4.
Load the Terrath palette as an Aseprite:
colour-palette.md holds 32 four-step ramps. Build it once as a palette file and load it into every sprite.

Palette panel > folder icon > Load Palette, then Save Palette so it appears in your presets.

Work from the palette, not the colour wheel. The point of a fixed palette is that two assets drawn a month apart still belong in the same game — picking a fresh colour each time guarantees they will not.
Pencil, eraser and bucket at 1 px with a:
B pencil, E eraser, G bucket. Confirm all three at brush size 1 with no anti-aliasing.

Anti-aliasing is the one setting that silently ruins pixel art: it produces semi-transparent edge pixels that are not in your palette and cannot be shaded. Check the bucket's Tolerance too — the default sometimes bleeds across a soft edge.

Turn on PIXEL-PERFECT mode on the pencil (it appears in the tool options when the pencil is selected). It removes the doubled corner pixels that make a hand-drawn line look lumpy.

Shift+click draws a straight line from the last point. X swaps foreground and background.
Selection, colour replace and shading mo:
M rectangular marquee, with the lasso and magic wand beside it. Ctrl+D deselects.

Edit > Replace Color swaps one palette entry everywhere in the selection — the fastest way to try a different shadow hue across a whole sprite.

SHADING MODE is the pencil's third ink mode, in the ink dropdown beside the brush size. With a palette ramp selected it shifts pixels ALONG the ramp instead of painting a flat colour, which is how you shade without hand-picking every step. It is the most useful thing in Aseprite that people never find.
Layers and groups — body, equipment, sha:
§3.1: "Layers should separate only things that require independent editing or runtime treatment — body, equipment, shadow and effects — not every small colour cluster."

Four layers, not twenty. A layer per colour cluster feels organised and turns every edit into a hunt through a stack.

Shift+N new layer; group with the folder icon. Alt+click a layer's eye to solo it — the fastest way to check whether equipment reads on its own.
Frames, tags, onion skin, and playback a:
Alt+N new frame. Comma and period step back and forward. Enter plays in a window; Shift+Enter plays on the canvas.

Set 12 fps: select all frames, right-click > Frame Properties, duration 83 ms. §5.1 and §5.2 both specify 12 fps, so every gameplay animation runs at this.

Onion skin is the icon above the timeline. Turn it on while drawing in-betweens — without it you are guessing at the frames either side.
A tag named lower-case snake-case, and o:
Select a frame range, right-click > New Tag. Name it action_direction in lower-case snake-case: idle_s, move_ne, staff_attack_1_se. §5.4 is explicit that names state the action and direction and never a sequence — no animation1, no walk2.

A leading underscore means one-shot: _hurt_s. Aseprite Wizard strips the underscore and imports it with looping disabled. §5.3.

One tag per file. §3.1 wants one master per asset, action and direction, so a file holds exactly one animation and the file name and the tag agree.
Export a sheet, and find where Aseprite:
File > Export Sprite Sheet. Aseprite Wizard reads the .aseprite file directly, so routine work needs no manual export at all — this is about knowing what it produces and where it lands.

§3.1: generated runtime sheets live under media/sprites/_exports/ and are NEVER edited by hand. If you ever find yourself fixing a pixel in an export, the master is wrong and that is where the fix belongs.
Learn the shortcuts for pencil, eyedropp:
The ones worth having in the hands rather than the menus:

- B pencil, E eraser, G bucket, M marquee, I eyedropper (or hold Alt with any tool)
- X swap foreground/background, Ctrl+Z undo
- Comma / period for previous / next frame, Alt+N new frame, Enter play
- Tab hides the whole UI, which is how you judge a sprite with no panels around it
- Shift+click for a straight line from the last point

Verify these against your build, then CUSTOMISE them in Edit > Keyboard Shortcuts. Defaults shift a little between versions, and the real gain is binding the four or five things you reach for every minute to keys your hand already knows.
Aseprite’s own docs, start to finish, on:
aseprite.org/docs. It is small — an afternoon, not a course.

Read it once deliberately rather than discovering features accidentally over a year. The things people miss and then need: shading ink mode, pixel-perfect, tilemap mode, custom brushes, selection modifiers, and the scripting API.

This ends the tool thread. Everything after is pixel art, which no menu teaches.
Draw at 1× only — every judgement made a:
§10.1: "Draw at native 1× resolution with deliberate clusters rather than resized or filtered source art."

Zoom in to place pixels; zoom OUT to decide anything. A sprite that looks good at 800% and muddy at 100% ships muddy, because 100% is what the game shows.

Keep a second view at 1× open (View > New View) beside the zoomed one and glance at it constantly. §5.3 requires every animation checked at native scale anyway, so build the habit now.
50 clean one-pixel lines at every angle,:
A clean pixel line has a consistent step pattern: 1:1 at 45°, then 2:1, 3:1, 1:2 and so on. An unclean one steps 2, then 3, then 2 — and the eye reads that as a wobble even at 1×.

Draw 50: horizontal, vertical, 45°, 2:1, 1:2, 3:1, 1:3, and awkward angles between. By hand with the pencil, not the line tool, then compare each against what the line tool produces.

The goal is a hand that makes even steps without thinking, because every outline you will ever draw is made of these.
The jaggy rule: 20 curves with no single:
A jaggy is a step that breaks a run — a curve going 3, 3, 2, 3 instead of 3, 3, 2, 2, 1. It reads as a dent in the form.

A good pixel curve has steps that change monotonically: 4, 3, 2, 1, 1, and never back up. Draw 20 curves of varying tightness and fix every step that breaks the run.

Pixel-perfect mode handles doubled corners and does nothing about this. It is the judgement the tool cannot make for you.
20 circles of different diameters, pixel:
Small circles are memorised shapes, not calculated ones. A clean 5, 7, 9 and 11 px circle each has one correct pixel arrangement, and you want them in your hand.

Draw them freehand, then compare with the ellipse tool. Where they differ, the tool is usually right about symmetry and wrong about weight.

Circles matter because heads, shoulders, wheels, coins, shields and every soft form start as one.
Recognise banding in someone else’s spri:
Banding is two colour bands running parallel along the same pixel step for a stretch, so the eye reads a stripe instead of a surface. It is the clearest tell of inexperienced pixel art and invisible until you learn to see it.

Find it first in art that is not yours — open any sprite sheet and look along the shading boundaries for parallel runs. Then find it in your own, which is harder.

The fix is to break the parallel: let the bands diverge, or shorten one run.
Deliberate clusters versus noise — redra:
§10.1 forbids "indiscriminate dithering, isolated noise and high-resolution texture imitation".

A cluster is a deliberate group of same-colour pixels with a readable shape. Noise is single pixels scattered to suggest texture. At 1× noise reads as dirt, and in motion it shimmers.

Take a patch you have textured with scattered pixels and redraw it as three or four clusters. It will look simpler and read better, which is the lesson.
Draw the same 32 × 32 object three times:
The exercise that teaches restraint faster than any reading.

1. Draw it the way you want to, detail everywhere.
2. Redraw with deliberate clusters and no isolated pixels.
3. Redraw again using visibly fewer pixels and fewer colours.

Look at all three at 1×. The third is almost always best, and finding that out from your own hand is the point. §2: "Silhouette, value separation, pose readability and ground contact take priority over decorative detail."
A sphere, a cube and a cylinder with key:
§10.1: "The authored key light comes from the upper-left; shadows and undersides favour the lower-right."

Every asset in the game is lit this way, so it has to become automatic. Draw the three primitives with a lit plane up-left, a mid tone across the form, a shadow down-right, and a core shadow where the form turns away — which is DARKER than the cast shadow, not lighter.

Four values, no more. These three forms are what every character and prop is made of.
Shadows and undersides favouring the low:
"Static shading stays restrained so Godot's local lights can read coherently." §10.1.

This is the constraint people get wrong. It is not a single-light painting; it is a sprite that will be lit AGAIN at runtime by Light2D. Bake in too much contrast and the game's own lighting fights it, and a torch-lit scene looks wrong.

Enough shading to describe the form, not enough to describe a specific scene. Err lighter than feels finished.
Four values of stone; four of cloth; fou:
Same four-value budget, four materials — the exercise is how the VALUE PATTERN differs, not the hue.

- Stone: hard edges between values, flat planes, a chipped silhouette
- Cloth: soft transitions, folds that follow gravity, a mid tone dominating
- Metal: high contrast, a narrow bright highlight, bounce light low on the form
- Wood: grain as a few long clusters, never per-pixel texture

If a material seems to need a fifth value, decide whether it is the material or your shading that is unclear.
20 materials at three or four purposeful:
§10.1: "approximately three or four purposeful values per major material. Avoid smooth gradients."

Twenty: stone, brick, thatch, plaster, iron, brass, leather, linen, wool, fur, bark, leaf, water, glass, bone, rope, clay, ash, snow, blood.

"Purposeful" is the operative word. Each value should MEAN something — lit plane, form turn, core shadow, bounce. If you cannot say what a value is for, you have four shades and not four values.
THE BLACK TEST: a sprite still identifia:
§10.1: "Every playable hero must remain identifiable in solid black, grayscale, dark lighting and a busy party scene."

Fill the sprite with one colour and look at it. Can you tell who it is? Which way it faces? What it is holding?

If not, the silhouette is the problem, and no amount of interior detail will fix it. This test decides whether a sprite works at all, and the tool cannot run it for you.

Fix it by changing the pose, the equipment outline, or the negative gaps — never by adding detail inside.
THE GREY TEST: the same sprite identifia:
Desaturate completely. Everything should still separate: body from equipment, limb from torso, character from ground.

"Identity cannot depend on hue, glow, jewellery or microscopic detail." §10.1. A character told apart only by being the red one disappears in darkness, in a crowd, and for a colourblind player.

If it fails, the fix is value separation — push one element lighter or darker — not a different colour.
Fix a sprite that fails both, and write:
Take something of yours that fails one or both tests and repair it. Then write the one sentence that says what the fix was.

The failures recur: silhouette collapsing at the shoulders, equipment the same value as the torso, a weapon vanishing against the body. Knowing which of your own habits causes it is worth more than knowing the rule.
Preserve negative gaps between body, lim:
§10.1: "Preserve useful negative gaps between body, limbs and equipment, and allow signature equipment to break the torso silhouette."

A gap of even one transparent pixel between arm and torso keeps the arm readable. Close it and the figure becomes a blob at 1×, especially in motion.

Take a figure with arms held close and open a one-pixel gap each side. Compare at 1×. The difference is larger than it has any right to be.
Read colour-palette.md and find the ramp:
colour-palette.md documents 32 four-step ramps — 128 base colours, plus a Nix Green ramp at TERR-129 to 132.

Note a known inconsistency in that file: line 16 says "exactly 32 four-step ramps and 128 approved base colours" and line 30 says "the 132 entries below". There is a Trello card for it. Do not let it confuse you.

Ramps, not swatches, is the point. A ramp is a material's four values already chosen to sit together, which is what makes two assets drawn weeks apart belong to one game. Find which ramps are warm, which cool, and which neutrals you will reach for constantly.
Shadows by hue shift, not by darkening a:
A shadow made by lowering brightness alone goes muddy. A good one shifts hue as it darkens — usually toward blue or purple under cool light, toward red under warm — and often drops saturation at the darkest end.

The palette's ramps already do this, which is most of why they exist. Compare: take a mid tone, darken it in the picker, and set it beside the ramp's own next-darker step. The ramp looks like a material; yours looks like the same colour turned down.
A one-pixel dark COLOURED outline — neve:
§10.1: "Use a dark coloured one-pixel outline. Avoid universal pure black."

Pure black everywhere makes every asset look stuck onto the scene, and it goes dead under coloured runtime light. A dark version OF THE ADJACENT COLOUR — dark brown against skin, dark blue against steel — holds the form and stays in the palette.

One pixel. Always one pixel.
No double outlines, and equipment never:
Two failures named explicitly in §10.1.

A double outline happens when you outline a part and then outline the whole: two pixels of line in places, one elsewhere, which reads as a smear.

Merging happens when equipment and torso share an outline, so a sword becomes part of the body. The fix is the negative gap from stage 3, or a value change across the boundary.
Choose a 12–18 colour subset for a hero:
§10.1: "A normal hero usually uses 12-18 opaque base colours... These are discipline ranges rather than reasons to discard a necessary material distinction."

Budget it: skin 3-4, hair 3, main garment 4, secondary garment 3, metal 3, outline colours 2. That is already 18.

The budget forces the decision of which materials matter enough to distinguish, and that is the exercise. Count the colours in the finished file and check.
Choose 4–10 for a small prop (§10.1):
A barrel, a crate, a lantern, a stool. Four to ten colours total, §10.1.

Props are where restraint is cheapest to learn and most obvious: the whole thing is one or two materials, so there is nowhere to hide an unnecessary colour.

Draw five props inside the budget. One of them should use only four.
Choose 8–26 for an ordinary enemy (§10.1:
The widest range in §10.1, because an enemy might be a plain bandit or a thing made of several materials.

Do one at each end: an enemy that works on 8, and one that genuinely needs 26. Being able to say WHY the second needs them is the lesson — if you cannot, it needs fewer.
Redraw one asset with six fewer colours:
Take a finished asset and remove six colours by merging the closest pairs.

Usually it loses nothing and reads better, because those colours were doing no work. Occasionally it loses a material distinction that mattered — and §10.1 is explicit that the ranges are "discipline ranges rather than reasons to discard a necessary material distinction", so that case is allowed.

Knowing which case you are in is the skill.
A prop in 4–10 colours, correct outline,:
The first complete asset to contract. A barrel or a crate.

Before calling it done: 4-10 colours, one-pixel dark coloured outline, three or four values per material, key light upper-left, no isolated pixels, judged at 1×, passes the black test.

Props are the right place to do this first because the whole contract applies while the subject is simple enough that only the contract is hard.
A character facing S: 112 × 112, pivot (:
§4: internal viewport 960 × 540, adult gameplay frame 112 × 112, pivot (56, 96), approximately 80 px sole-to-crown.

80 px for a whole human is not much — roughly 10 px for the head. Everything must be decided: eyes are one or two pixels, a hand is three across. Budget the figure in head-heights before drawing a pixel.

§4 also warns that measured height varies with pose — the approved idle reaches 81-87 px by direction — so 80 is the standard, not a number to normalise every frame to.
Stable ground contact, and a pose that k:
Two rules from §4, and the second is the subtle one.

"Ground contact must be stable in every frame." The feet sit at the pivot and do not drift between frames unless the character is moving.

"A pose that crouches, falls or lies down keeps the same anatomical scale as its upright pose. Never normalize each frame's bounding-box height independently; doing so makes prone bodies grow." A lying figure drawn to fill the frame becomes a giant. Draw it at the scale it would be standing.
Signature equipment that breaks the tors:
"Allow signature equipment to break the torso silhouette." §10.1.

A crook, a staff, a satchel, a brimmed hat — something that reaches past the body so the character is identifiable in solid black from shape alone.

This is how heroes stay distinguishable in a party scene, and it is a design decision rather than a rendering one. Run the black test: can you name the character from the silhouette?
The same character in all eight authored:
§5.1 and §5.4: eight separately authored directions — S, SE, E, NE, N, NW, W, SW — and no mirroring. §5.4 permits mirroring only for an explicitly approved asset "whose handedness, costume and action geometry survive the flip", which for a character carrying something in one hand it does not.

Eight drawings, not four and a flip. The back views are the hard ones and the ones people skip, so do them first.

This is the largest single piece of work in character art and the reason asset counts are what they are.
Readability in a busy party scene and in:
The last two of §10.1's four readability conditions, and the ones needing a real scene rather than a canvas.

Put the sprite in the game beside other characters, then under a Light2D at low intensity. Both are tests the sprite can only fail in context.

If it disappears in a crowd, the silhouette or value structure is too close to its neighbours. If it disappears in the dark, the shading was baked too heavily — see stage 3.
An asset brief written BEFORE the next a:
§10.2: "Before drawing, an asset brief identifies its subject, states, directions, actions, frame geometry, anchor, palette subset and runtime consumer. Anything with no accepted on-screen use is not a production requirement yet."

Eight fields on one page, before any pixels. It prevents the two expensive mistakes: drawing something nothing uses, and drawing something at the wrong geometry.

"There is no master speculative sprite catalogue." Requirements come from accepted content — systems.md, the current brief, characters.md, the interface contracts. If nothing on screen needs it, do not draw it.
The approved idle, one direction: 24 fra:
§5.1 exactly: 24 frames at 12 fps, looping for two seconds, 112 × 112, pivot (56, 96).

Two seconds is long for an idle, deliberately — it stops the loop reading as a twitch. Every frame at 83 ms.

Start with S and get the loop seamless before authoring the other seven. Watch it at 1× for a full minute; loop faults only show on the third or fourth repeat.
Three to five meaningful poses, with the:
§5.1: "3-5 meaningful poses, with the approved held portion and loop drop preserved."

Not 24 different drawings — three to five poses with holds between them. The held portion is where the character is nearly still, which is most of the two seconds. The loop drop is the settle that returns to the start without a visible jump.

media/reference/Animation/README.md documents the intended variation per direction. Read it before authoring: the approved reference IS the contract for idle motion.
The idle in all eight directions, author:
Eight separate 24-frame animations. No mirroring. §5.1.

192 frames for one character's idle — the honest cost, and why §10.2 insists on a brief first.

Do S, then N, before any diagonal. They are the two hardest and most different; if those work, the rest follow in judgement if not in pixels.
The approved run, one direction: 12 fram:
§5.2: 12 frames, currently played at 12 fps, 112 × 112, pivot (56, 96).

Twelve frames is one second of run — in practice two strides of six. The contact, down, pass and up positions are the four that carry it; the rest are in-betweens.

Ground contact is the thing to get right. §4: stable in every frame. A run where the feet slide is the most common animation fault there is.
The run in eight directions, legs moveme:
Eight authored directions, no mirroring. §5.2.

"Movement-facing legs" means the legs always face where the character is going. That is what keeps locomotion readable regardless of where the character is aiming.
Upper body aim-facing, at most two direc:
§5.2 and §5.4: upper body faces the aim, legs face the movement, and the two differ by AT MOST two of the eight direction steps — 90 degrees.

Beyond that the body twists impossibly, so the constraint is anatomical rather than arbitrary. Past the limit, the legs turn instead.

"The true aim remains represented by the ground arrow." §5.4 — the sprite does not carry the whole burden of showing aim, which is why 90 degrees is enough.
A one-shot action: anticipation, active:
§5.3: "Anticipation, active frames, impacts, release moments and recovery must match gameplay timing."

Four phases, and their frame counts come from the ACTION's timing in systems.md, not from what looks smooth: anticipation (the wind-up the player reads), active (the frames that hit), impact (the stop), recovery (the return to idle).

"Smoothness never overrides responsiveness." §5.4. If the anticipation is longer than the game allows, cut frames — not responsiveness.
Tag it with a leading _ so it imports wi:
_staff_attack_1_se. The underscore is the whole mechanism: Aseprite Wizard strips it and imports with looping off. §5.3.

Locomotion and idle loop. Attacks, interactions, reactions and downing do not. Get it wrong and an attack repeats forever — immediately obvious, trivially fixed, but only if you know the rule exists.
Check every animation at native scale, i:
§5.3: "Every animation is checked at native scale, in motion, against the real ground and under representative lighting."

Four conditions, none of which a canvas provides. In Aseprite an animation can look fine and still be wrong in the game, because the canvas has no ground, no neighbours and no light.

Make this the last step of every animation, not an occasional check.
A telegraph that reads through pose and:
§5.3: "Telegraphs must read through pose, silhouette, motion and sound rather than colour alone."

A telegraph is the frames that warn the player what is coming. If the warning is a colour flash it fails in darkness, in a crowd, and for a colourblind player — the grey test again, in motion.

Test it: desaturate the animation and play it. Can you still tell the attack is coming?
Masters under media/sprites/<category>/<:
§3.1 exactly: media/sprites/<category>/<family>/<asset-key>/ — for example media/sprites/characters/sheep/sheep-a/.

The structure matters because §3 requires one unambiguous editable master per asset. A file in the wrong place becomes a second master, and then nobody knows which is current.

media/reference/ holds reference material only and "never a second editable master". §3.1.
Named <asset-key>_<action>_<direction>.a:
sheep-a_walk_ne.aseprite, containing one tag: walk_ne.

File name and tag say the same thing on purpose — the importer reads the tag, a human reads the name, and they cannot disagree.

One master per asset, action AND direction. §3.1. Eight directions of a walk is eight files, not one file with eight tags.
Names that state action and direction —:
§5.4: "Naming states the action and direction plainly: idle_s, move_ne, staff_attack_1_se. Do not use sequence names such as animation1 or walk2."

A sequence name tells you nothing six months later. walk2 — second what? Faster? A different character? A second attempt?

Not pedantry: it is the difference between a media folder you can navigate and one you have to open file by file.
Import through Aseprite Wizard to Sprite:
The proven route, confirmed working on the rig: Aseprite Wizard imports .aseprite masters straight to Godot SpriteFrames, one animation per file, tagged action_direction.

§3: "Accepted .aseprite masters import through Aseprite Wizard; no competing sprite export pipeline is established." This is the only route; a second one would create a second source of truth.

The binary is at ~/Games/steam/steamapps/common/Aseprite/aseprite and the Godot editor setting points at it. Note that ~/Games is a symlink into the mergerfs pool, so if the pool drops the binary appears to vanish and the path looks broken when it is not.
Exports land in media/sprites/_exports/:
§3.1. A derived file is derived: if a pixel is wrong in an export, the master is wrong.

The temptation is real — the export is right there and the fix is one pixel. Do it once and the master and the game disagree forever, with nothing recording which is correct.

§3: "Generated exports and Godot imports are derived files, not alternative masters."
See it in Godot at native scale under Li:
The actual finish line. Not "it looks right in Aseprite" — it looks right in the game.

Load it into the scene it belongs in, at native scale, under that scene's lighting, beside what it will appear beside. §2: "Gameplay must remain readable at native scale during movement, combat, crowds, darkness and effects."

Everything in stages 3 and 4 about restrained shading exists for this moment. If the sprite goes flat or muddy here, go back to the values.
One unambiguous editable master, and the:
The rule that holds the pipeline together and is the most easily lost.

§3: "An accepted asset has one unambiguous editable master." And bluntly: "Rejected and superseded art is deleted rather than archived."

That second one is deliberate. An archived old version is a second master waiting to be opened by mistake. Delete it — git has it if it ever matters.
Study one Eastward screenshot for value:
§2 names Eastward and Sea of Stars as informing "composition and value organization", then immediately adds: "they are references, not templates. Individual scenes, designs and incidental details from any reference are not copied."

So the study is structural. Take one screenshot and desaturate it. Where are the darkest darks? How many values is the background using versus the characters? How is the character separated from the ground — outline, value, or a gap?

Write three sentences about the value structure. Do not copy a single asset.
Study one Sea of Stars screenshot the sa:
Same method, different answers. Sea of Stars is more saturated, uses more values per material than Eastward, and lets its lighting do more work.

The comparison is the lesson: two games both called excellent pixel art, organising value and colour quite differently. Which is closer to §2's "warm, earthy, weathered environments and strong landmark silhouettes"?

Again: references, not templates. §2.
Draw the sheep walk masters — the Highfo:
The first real production job, and it is already specified.

.aseprite masters for sheep-a, one file per action and direction, in media/sprites/. Five authored directions (e, n, ne, s, se); SheepSpriteBody drives eight-way facing from those five and picks graze / idle / walk / trot / alert-bleat from behaviour. WALK is what the Highfold needs first.

Canon is waiting on this too: canon/species/sheep.md has its Appearance section deliberately left pending the art, and the Trello card sits in Waiting.
Draw the real menu window art and retire:
media/ui/menu/inventorywindow.png is the one documented placeholder inside otherwise-approved UI art, drawn behind all eight menu tabs.

Two things mark it out: it is the only file in media/ui/ with no alpha channel, and it has a near-black margin baked into the edge — which is why the "black box" appeared.

Two constants die with it. MenuPage.WINDOW_REGION and WINDOW_BORDER exist only to crop that baked margin, and the window test deliberately FAILS if a clean file arrives while the crop is still in, so it will tell you. The menu ink recolour is parked until this lands.

§8: HUD and UI art uses transparent PNG and does not inherit sprite canvas, pivot or animation rules.
Replace one greybox terrain placeholder:
§11: "Draw approved terrain and character/creature masters to replace the current code and greybox placeholders."

Pick one terrain piece and take it all the way: brief, draw, import, see it in the scene under light. Read §9.1 and §9.2 on asset classes, projection and world scale first, and §9.3 on environment drawing and validation.

One piece finished properly teaches more than five started.
Draw one prop to contract, start to fini:
The proficiency test. A prop, from asset brief to Godot, in one sitting, hitting every clause of §10.1 without looking them up.

If you have to check the colour range, the outline rule or the light direction, you are not there yet — draw more props. When it is automatic, the contract has stopped being a checklist and become how you draw.
One asset a week, to contract, reviewed:
Ongoing, and the only thing that makes the rest stick.

One asset a week, reviewed against §10.1 before it counts as done: values per material, outline, light direction, the black test, the grey test, crowd, darkness, colour count.

§10 is called "Validation and definition of done" for a reason. An asset is not done because it is finished; it is done because it passes.
